papers.title: ADfiRe: An empirical- and CFD-informed advection-diffusion-reaction thermal model for wildfire spread
papers.abstract: Real-time wildfire forecasting requires a trade-off between rapid yet physically relevant models and high fidelity but computationally costly models of flame spread over heterogeneous, multiphase solid fuel. The present study introduces ADfiRe, a hybrid framework that integrates empirical correlations and CFD-informed parameterizations into a physics-based advection-diffusion-reaction (ADR) formulation. The key features of ADfiRe are the use of established fuel databases, the capacity to handle multiple fuels, and a methodology to capture the effect of arbitrary topography. Furthermore, it includes the effect of flame tilting due to wind, thus accounting for the differences between plume- and wind-dominated fire propagation. ADfiRe resolves explicitly the coupled thermochemical degradation as well as heat and mass transport mechanisms of the advancing fire front. The wind field is modeled based on an appropriately defined Byram number. The model is validated against five well-documented experimental field-scale fires in Mediterranean shrublands, showing quantitative agreement with key metrics such as the rate of spread (ROS) and the fireline intensity, through a two-stage, Arrhenius-based heterogeneous reaction scheme coupling solid-fuel pyrolysis and oxygen-limited char/volatile combustion.

papers.title: Wavelet Flow Matching for Multi-Scale Physics Emulation
papers.abstract: Accurate emulation of multi-scale physical systems governed by PDEs demands models that remain stable over long autoregressive rollouts while preserving fine-scale structures. Deterministic emulators produce overly smoothed predictions, while generative approaches better capture details but are costly. Latent-space generative models have emerged as a compromise but with the additional cost of separately pre-trained autoencoders. We propose Wavelet Flow Matching (WFM), a generative emulator that overcomes current trade-offs between cost and skill by performing optimal-transport flow matching directly in the multi-scale wavelet space. Rather than learning a latent compression, WFM leverages the hierarchical structure of a U-Net to jointly predict the transport velocities of a prescribed, lossless wavelet representation. On three challenging systems of chaotic fluid dynamics, WFM achieves superior spectral coherence and competitive or better long-horizon accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models. Our results position the wavelet space as an effective training-free representation for generative emulation of complex physical dynamics.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $\phi$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $\phi$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $\phi$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $\phi$-PICT is publicly available at https://github.com/upb-sciml/phiPICT.

papers.title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
authors: Jun Fang (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
Ling Zou (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
Rui Hu (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
papers.abstract: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

papers.title: The Benjamin-Feir stability diagram for Stokes waves with constant vorticity in finite depth
papers.abstract: We determine the Benjamin-Feir stability diagram for small-amplitude Stokes waves with constant vorticity in finite depth. For the full water wave system, we derive an explicit instability index and rigorously classify its sign throughout the depth-vorticity plane. With gravitational acceleration and carrier wavenumber normalized to one, we identify a unique minimum depth $h_{\text{crit}}\approx1.36271$, below which Benjamin-Feir instability is absent for every vorticity. Above this depth, two vorticity thresholds delimit the unstable regime, outside of which the spectrum near the origin remains purely imaginary for all small Floquet exponents. In particular, at each fixed finite depth, constant vorticity of sufficiently large magnitude suppresses Benjamin-Feir instability. Moreover, any constant vorticity $\gamma\ge 2/\sqrt{3}$ suppresses Benjamin-Feir instability at every finite depth. The proof combines Hamiltonian spectral perturbation theory, symbolic computations, and formal verification in Rocq. Away from the transition set, our results rigorously confirm the stability criterion predicted by the nonlinear Schr\"odinger approximation of Thomas, Kharif, and Manna.

papers.title: Remarks on Souriau's Geometric Thermodynamics for Weak Two-Dimensional Euler Flows
papers.abstract: We examine infinitesimal symmetries of relative entropy on low-regularity vorticity spaces and compare them with symmetries of stationary laws of weak two-dimensional Euler trajectories. Relative-entropy invariance under sample-space transformations is equivalent to preservation of the reference law; the corresponding weak infinitesimal condition is a vanishing reference-divergence identity. White-noise vorticity has an infinite-dimensional family of such symmetries, generated by smooth area-preserving transport. At the level of path laws, however, marginal entropy symmetries need not preserve temporal correlations. We first give a continuous Gaussian counterexample, including its infinitesimal form. We then establish a counterexample directly for stationary white-noise weak Euler path laws: explicit non-isometric area-preserving shears preserve the white-noise marginal but cannot preserve an Euler path law satisfying the standard symmetrized weak vorticity equation. We also examine the reduction of guaranteed entropy symmetries under conditioning by renormalized energy. These observations distinguish thermodynamic symmetry, Hamiltonian covariance, and statistical path dynamics without asserting a selection principle for nonunique weak solutions.

papers.title: Global saddle selection and exact absolute-instability boundaries for convection in porous media with throughflow
papers.abstract: In the Darcy-Prats problem, horizontal throughflow leaves the temporal onset of convection unchanged but raises the heating required for a localized disturbance to grow at a fixed point. The saddle equations give five candidates, but only the saddles reached by deformation of the Fourier contour contribute to the growth. For $Ra>\pi^2$, $Pe>0$ we prove that the same off-axis pair contributes throughout the domain: no Stokes transition can change its contribution. Its growth gives a unique analytic absolute threshold, first reached by the lowest vertical mode. Rescaling transfers the selection to Forchheimer drag, transverse rolls of a power-law fluid, anisotropic permeability, an open upper boundary and a vertical magnetic field. A shift of the same growth function accounts for interphase heat exchange in a model of metallic foam. At prescribed throughflow the threshold increases strictly with either resistance coefficient. In particular, a vertical magnetic field raises the absolute threshold at fixed P\'eclet number. Tabulated thresholds check the reduction. Algebraic elimination gives the boundary polynomial, and frequency recovery selects its physical branch. At the Darcy level the selected saddles trace an arc of the elliptic curve 11a3, a degeneration of a genus-two family at nonzero shifted levels. Series inversion on this arc gives an integer weak-throughflow series and an all-order strong-throughflow expansion. Rational certificates establish the exact convergence radii of both series on the selected sheets.

papers.title: Potential Flow, Stress, and Straightness in Flow Matching: Euler Error on Gaussian-Mixture Targets
papers.abstract: In linear flow matching, coupling straightness measures conditional displacement variance. The conditional covariance gives a kinetic stress in the Jeans balance. The virial identity relates the mean trace of the covariance to a radial moment of acceleration. Euler error also depends on how the flow propagates acceleration. On constructed Gaussian-mixture targets, closed-form couplings with matched straightness yield different median Euler errors. Learned fields from fresh minibatch assignments also yield different Euler errors from their partners at matched estimated straightness. The leading Euler coefficient accounts for more of the error variation than straightness in these experiments. We relate the additive-noise characterization of isotropic Gaussian sources to potential flow. A gradient constraint reduces velocity error on the independent isotropic Gaussian example and increases it on two examples with rotational exact fields.

papers.title: Hydr\'oDex: gotta match 'em all!
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive hydrodynamic classification of stationary fluid profiles in first-order phase transitions within the constant-sound-speed model, a physically motivated extension of the standard bag model that allows the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the bubble wall and evolving the profile in the surrounding plasma, we systematically identify and classify all the possible stationary solutions. The classification recovers all previously known direct and inverse detonation, deflagration, and hybrid solutions, while revealing a new class of stationary configurations, termed mixed hybrids, featuring rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+ > c_-$, the classification in terms of the wall velocity $\xi_w$ and the asymptotic strength parameter $\alpha_N$ further exhibits degenerate regions in parameter space, where multiple distinct stationary profiles correspond to the same physical inputs $(\xi_w,\alpha_N)$. This non-uniqueness arises as the parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We also compute the kinetic-energy budget and the associated acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed-hybrid solutions, despite their oppositely directed flows, introduce no additional spectral feature, and their spectra can be closely mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with very different fluid profiles. Finally, we release Hydr\'oDex, a public code that implements the complete hydrodynamic classification, fluid-profile construction, kinetic-energy budget, and gravitational-wave calculation.

papers.title: Influence of transverse oscillatory shear on the viscous fingering instability
papers.abstract: Oscillatory shear can delay the onset of viscous fingering. In addition, uniaxial translational shear also breaks the symmetry of the resulting pattern so that the interface evolves differently depending on its direction of propagation relative to the shear axis. We observe a delayed fingering onset and reduced subsequent finger growth rate for all directions as shear speed or amplitude increases. However, shear widens fingers growing in the direction perpendicular to shear and elongates those in the parallel directions. After onset, neighboring fingers in the perpendicular directions can reconnect near their base when the shear amplitude exceeds approximately five times the excess linear finger wavelength at the onset. Concentration profiles reveal smoother azimuthal edges and overlapping structures behind the tips. These observations show that shear smears individual fingers and connects neighboring ones. This correlates lateral fingering interactions with radial propagation.

papers.title: Catenaries in viscous fluid
papers.abstract: This work explores a simple model of a slender, flexible structure in a uniform flow, providing analytical solutions for the translating, axially flowing equilibria of strings subjected to a uniform body force and drag forces linear in the velocities. The classical catenaries are extended to a five-parameter family of curves. A sixth parameter affects the tension in the curves. Generic configurations are planar, represented by a single first order equation for the tangential angle. The effects of varying parameters on representative shapes, orbits in angle-curvature space, and stress distributions are shown. As limiting cases, the solutions include configurations corresponding to "lariat chains" and the towing, reeling, and sedimentation of flexible cables in a highly viscous fluid. Regions of parameter space corresponding to infinitely long, semi-infinite, and finite length curves are delineated. Almost all curves subtend an angle less than $\pi$ radians, but curious special cases with doubled or infinite range occur on the borders between regions. Separate transitions in the tension behavior, and counterintuitive results regarding finite towing tensions for infinitely long cables, are presented. Several physically inspired boundary value problems are solved and discussed.

papers.title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
papers.abstract: Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.

papers.title: Breaking-induced energy dissipation of surface gravity waves at varying scales and co-flowing wind stresses
authors: Enrique M. Padilla (Universitat Polit\`ecnica de Catalunya)
papers.abstract: Breaking-induced energy dissipation is studied for individual unsteady breaking waves using laboratory measurements of unidirectional surface gravity wave groups across a range of wave scales and wind stresses. A refined framework to estimate breaking-induced dissipation $\Delta E_{br}$ is proposed that accounts for background dissipation from non-breaking processes. Using this framework, we show that variations in wave scale primarily influence breaking energetics, such as fractional dissipation $\Delta E_{br}/E_0$ and dissipation rate $\epsilon_b$, by modifying the breaking onset threshold. Also, co-flowing wind systematically reduces both $\Delta E_{br}/E_0$ and $\epsilon_b$ relative to unforced conditions, as wind-forced waves break earlier with reduced crest forward-leaning. Exploiting the crest-front steepness at incipient breaking $\mathcal{S}_{\text{front}}(t_b)$ to characterise breaking onset and local crest geometry, we formulate a scaling for $\epsilon_b$ based on this local measure. This then yields $\Delta E_{br}/E_0 \propto \beta^{*}\,\mathcal{S}_b\,(\tau_b/T_b)$, where $\beta^{*}$ is crest forward leaning, $\mathcal{S}_b$ local steepness, and $\tau_b/T_b$ non-dimensional breaking duration. This scaling highlights the important roles of crest asymmetry and breaking duration in setting the breaking energy dissipation. Finally, we consider the breaking strength parameter $b$ by assessing existing steepness-based scaling laws, and relate $b$ to $\mathcal{S}_{\text{front}}(t_b)$, yielding an approximately linear dependence once the breaking-onset threshold is considered.

papers.title: Solute pulse compression and spreading in power-law fluid flow through a semipermeable tube
papers.abstract: We investigate Taylor-Aris dispersion and filtration-induced compression of a solute pulse transported by a power-law fluid through a slender, semipermeable, circular tube. The wall permits solvent filtration, modelled by Starling's law, while completely retaining the solute. Lubrication theory and multiple-scale homogenisation yield a one-dimensional macrotransport equation with spatially varying effective advection and dispersion coefficients. An evolution equation for the axial variance identifies the competing contributions of mean-flow deceleration, dispersive spreading, and wall-induced concentration redistribution. Filtration causes the mean axial velocity to decrease downstream, allowing compressive advection to overcome dispersive spreading. A local critical-width criterion distinguishes instantaneous pulse contraction from spreading. We evaluate the contraction threshold using the integral variance balance and compare the predictions with axisymmetric convection-diffusion simulations. As the relative contributions of compression and dispersion evolve, an initially contracting pulse may reach a minimum width and subsequently spread. Power-law rheology modifies both the hydraulic field and the Taylor dispersion contribution. Under the reference conditions investigated, shear thinning produces greater cumulative pulse narrowing than the Newtonian case: at dimensionless time T=100, the pulse width decreases from its initial value by approximately 31 percent for flow behaviour index n=0.4, compared with 26 percent for n=1. Substantial pulse narrowing can coexist with an outlet solvent flow rate that is only a small fraction of the inlet value.

papers.title: Sign-switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature of liquid jets by microscopic laser-induced cavitation
papers.abstract: Localized forcing of liquid jets can trigger Rayleigh-Plateau breakup at low perturbation amplitudes or explosive fragmentation at high amplitudes, while controlled bending in the intermediate regime has remained unexplored. We show that femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation, seeded at the interface of a 100 micrometre-diameter water jet, produces a selectable curvature in 0.4-1 mm long segments. Cavitation rupturing at the liquid-air interface drives fast outward jetting and induces a slower recoil on the opposite boundary, which evolves on the capillary-inertial timescale and results in curving of the liquid segment. The curvature is governed by three laser parameters. Off-axis laser illumination on the jet shifts the refractive caustics and redistributes energy deposition between the front and rear interfaces. The resulting recoil imbalance determines the curvature sign, with a straight configuration in the balanced case. Laser energy offers additional control over the recoil impulse via plasma defocusing and nonlinear absorption in the liquid jet, where the response is bounded by axisymmetric deformation at low energy and explosive vaporization at high energy. Repetition rate sets the spacing between successive cavitation events and hence the length of the bent segment. Curvature extends across the segment for lengths of 6-10 jet diameters; shorter segments undergo Rayleigh-Plateau breakup, whereas longer ones bend mainly near their retracting ends. Our results offer a platform for optofluidic control of switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature in flowing liquid jets.

papers.title: Near-wall sedimentation of short cylinders at low Reynolds numbers: Translational and angular velocity models and experimental validation
papers.abstract: The sedimentation of short cylinders near rigid walls involves coupled translational and rotational motion, for which readily applicable kinematic descriptions remain limited. In this study, theoretical expressions for the translational and angular velocities were derived by combining slender-body theory, semi-empirical finite-aspect-ratio corrections, and hydrodynamic descriptions of fluid inertia and wall effects. The resulting expressions were assessed through time-resolved sedimentation experiments with rigid cylinders of mean aspect ratios $\bar{\chi}\approx3.8$--$5.8$ in a rectangular duct at particle Reynolds numbers of $Re_{\mathrm P}\approx O(10^{-1})$. The experiments revealed distinct near-wall trajectories, including non-contact glancing motion and contact-induced flipping. For glancing trajectories, the predicted translational and angular velocities reproduced the principal features of the measured kinematics, with good qualitative and, over substantial parts of the trajectories, quantitative agreement. The comparisons also identified different ranges of applicability for the investigated wall corrections and showed that wall-induced effects dominated the angular velocity under the conditions studied. The resulting, experimentally validated expressions provide readily applicable estimates of the instantaneous translational and angular velocities of short cylinders near rigid walls and a reference for investigating additional influences on their sedimentation dynamics, including lower Reynolds numbers and particle or wall elasticity.

papers.title: Flow structure, heat transport, and dissipation in vertical-field magnetoconvection at similar Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: We employ direct numerical simulations to investigate the effect of a vertical magnetic field on the flow structures, heat transport, and dissipation rates in Rayleigh--B\'enard convection of a low-Prandtl-number fluid ($\mathrm{Pr} = 0.025$) at an approximately fixed Reynolds number ($\mathrm{Re} \approx 880$), maintained by adjusting the Rayleigh number to compensate for the Lorentz force. As the Hartmann number increases, the flow becomes more anisotropic, which strengthens the positive convective heat fluxes relative to the negative ones and thereby raises the Nusselt number, accompanied by a thinning of the thermal boundary layers. The total viscous and thermal dissipation rates are dominated by the boundary layers, whereas the total magnetic dissipation rate is dominated by the bulk. With increasing Hartmann number, the boundary-layer fraction of the viscous and magnetic dissipation rates increases, whereas that of the thermal dissipation computed from the temperature fluctuations decreases, owing to the suppression of temperature fluctuations near the boundary layers. The dissipation rates deviate from log-normality and are well described by stretched exponential distributions, whose tails become more extended with increasing Hartmann number.

papers.title: Compressible gas flow through porous media under forced pressure and fluxes: compressibility number and pressure curvature
papers.abstract: Gas compressibility induces a nonlinear relationship between boundary forcing and pressure evolution in porous media. This matters in operations and experiments where inlet pressure, volumetric flux or mass flux is controlled, as each forcing produces a distinct transient approach to steady state. We analyze this systematically for isothermal gas flow, using the porous medium equation (PME), nondimensionalized in terms of a Peclet-type number $\Pi$ that compares the time scales of gas flow and pressure diffusion and measures the steady flow compression. At steady state, increasing $\Pi$ leads to a boundary layer near the outlet, of width $\sim\Pi^{-1}$, where the velocity and flow expansion scale as $\Pi$ and $\Pi^2$, respectively. Since $\Pi$ fixes the steady compression for all three inlet conditions, their transients can be compared directly. We derive a semi-analytical perturbation series in $\beta=2\Pi/(1+2\Pi)<1$, valid for the three inlet conditions, which remains convergent at large $\Pi$. Numerical solutions for $10^{-2}\leq\Pi\leq10^3$ show that the effective pressure-squared diffusivity plateaus at boundary-condition-dependent values for $\Pi\ll1$, and scales as $\Pi^{1/2}$ for $\Pi\gg1$, explained by the slowest eigenmode of the linearized PME about its steady state. To resolve local flow compression, we introduce the pressure curvature, $\kappa=\nabla^2 p$, and interpret its evolution through a nonlinear advection-diffusion-reaction equation. Curvature fields reveal localized compression pulses that migrate downstream and dissipate as the system relaxes, while curvature moments highlight a $\Pi$-dependent crossover from compression- to expansion-dominated transients. Applications to gas chromatography and underground hydrogen storage are illustrated.

papers.title: Active flow control based on topological data analysis and a DMDc reduced-order model for drag reduction
papers.abstract: Controlling and reducing undesirable vortical structures in unsteady flows is a major issue in aerodynamics. This paper presents an active control methodology that combines topological data analysis (TDA) through persistence diagrams, a reduced-order model based on dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) and receding-horizon model predictive control (MPC). Vortices are detected and characterised by the persistence diagram of the absolute value of the vorticity, which makes it possible to define a target flow in which only the useful vortices are retained. This target flow is computed offline in the reduced space by gradient descent, the derivative of a persistence diagram being defined through a parametrisation of the space of diagrams. The control loop then reduces to a small-dimensional convex quadratic program, whose construction we detail and whose cost we compare with that of an approach that places the diagrams directly in the cost function. The approach is applied numerically to the flow around an oscillating aircraft wing for seven vibration frequencies, and yields a mean reduction of the drag coefficient while preserving the main vortices.

papers.title: The effect of particle shape on sunlight exposure in a wind-driven free-surface flow
papers.abstract: We investigate how nonspherical marine particles, such as microplastics, phytoplankton, and ice, are exposed to sunlight near the water surface in wind-driven surface boundary layer conditions. We measure the depth and orientation of these particles in a laboratory wind-wave tank, then use this data to model how much sunlight the particles would be exposed to in an aquatic environment. In particular, we explore how their orientation affects their sunlight exposure in these conditions, since most studies to date do not account for orientation, turbulent shear flow, and wind-waves at the water surface. We find that in all cases, particles prefer certain orientations, and this causes the average sunlight exposure of the particles to be 5 to 40\% higher than would be expected if their orientations were random. Further, we find that the mean irradiance depends on the ratio of the particle mixing length $L_m$ to the light decay lengthscale $\lambda$, and the nature of this dependence differs between disks and rods. Disks experience disproportionately greater mean irradiance at smaller $L_m/\lambda$ due to the vertical variation in their orientations. These results have important implications for accurately estimating the sunlight exposure of particles in the surface boundary layer.

papers.title: Fully implicit timestepping methods for the rotating shallow water equations
papers.abstract: Fully implicit timestepping methods have had limited application in geophysical fluid dynamics due to challenges of finding suitable iterative solvers, since the coupled treatment of advection prevents the standard elimination techniques. However, overlapping Additive Schwarz methods provide a robust, scalable iterative approach for solving the monolithic coupled system for all fields and Runge-Kutta stages. In this study we investigate this approach applied to the rotating shallow water equations, facilitated by the Irksome package which provides automated code generation for implicit Runge-Kutta methods. We compare various schemes in terms of accuracy and efficiency using an implicit/explicit splitting method, namely the ARK2 scheme of Giraldo et al (2013), as a benchmark. This provides an initial look at whether implicit Runge-Kutta methods can be viable for atmosphere and ocean simulation.

papers.title: Inertial forces and elastohydrodynamic interaction of spherical particles in wall-bounded sedimentation experiments at low particle Reynolds number
papers.abstract: Unsteady, wall-bounded sedimentation of spheres at low particle Reynolds numbers under the influence of small elastic deformation was investigated experimentally. The complete kinematics of elastic and rigid spheres sedimenting from rest at various initial distances from a rigid plane wall in a rectangular duct were measured. Several previously unrecognized phenomena arising from fluid inertia and superimposed elastohydrodynamic effects were identified and analyzed. Among these is an \textit{inertial wall attraction}, whereby particles migrate towards the wall during the initial acceleration phase. After this initial phase, rigid spheres sedimenting at $Re_\text{P}\approx O(10^{-1})$ followed behavior consistent with classic wall-lift models, including approximately linear migration away from the wall. In contrast, at smaller Reynolds numbers, $Re_\text{P}\approx O(10^{-2})$, both rigid and elastic spheres exhibited persistently unsteady sedimentation, characterized by deceleration despite increasing wall distance. These results enable the formulation of a conceptual framework that classifies near-wall sedimentation regimes according to particle Reynolds number and the position of boundaries relative to the Stokes length scale. For increasing deformability, the unsteady behavior was further modulated by nonlinearities. The observations suggest the presence of an \textit{elastohydrodynamic memory} effect arising from the coupling of fluid inertial forces with particle deformability. The experimental findings are supported by computational fluid dynamics simulations that provide qualitative insight into the evolving flow field. Overall, the results demonstrate that classic assumptions commonly applied to particle sedimentation in creeping flows break down in the presence of nearby boundaries...

papers.title: Nonhomogeneous elastic turbulence in the two-dimensional Taylor-Couette flow
papers.abstract: Elastic turbulence is a spatially and temporally disordered flow state appearing in viscoelastic fluids at vanishing fluid inertia and large elasticity. The resulting flows have broad technological interest, particularly to enhance mixing and heat transfer in microdevices. Although its experimental characterization is now well established in different setups, its theoretical understanding and numerical reproducibility remain challenging, especially in wall-bounded geometries. By means of numerical simulations, we investigate the onset of elastic turbulence and the characteristics of the developed turbulent-like states in the two-dimensional, confined, Taylor-Couette system. First, we characterize the purely elastic instability, addressing previously contrasting evidence. We then show that the fully nonlinear dynamics are weakly anisotropic and strongly nonhomogeneous. Indeed, they are confined in a dynamically active region adjacent to the inner wall, akin to the elastic boundary layer from previous predictions. Within this region, in spite of some non-negligible deviations due to the nonhomogeneity of our setup, the statistical and spectral turbulent properties are to a reasonable extent not far from the theoretical expectations and experimental observations.

papers.title: On the wake and flapping dynamics of different aspect ratio flags
papers.abstract: The flapping of flags is a classical problem involving fast, large amplitude deformations of a thin flexible plate and unsteady flow phenomena. We perform systematic time- and space-resolved measurements of the deformation and drag acting on flapping flags for various aspect ratios and mass ratios. Flag deformations travel from the root to the tip while growing in amplitude. We present a robust method to determine the travelling wave properties, and reveal that the dimensionless wavelength $\lambda/L$ is constant for a given flutter mode, and that the wave speed equals the freestream velocity for aspect ratios above unity but decreases with decreasing mass and aspect ratio. We provide a mechanistic explanation of the influence of mass and aspect ratio on the flapping dynamics by introducing a mass-ratio-corrected dimensionless wave speed, which is proportional to the square root of the dynamic pressure difference across the flag. At smaller aspect ratio, the local dynamic pressure exerted by the fluid on the flag is reduced, leading to a decrease in the wave propagation speed and the tip frequency. Based on near wake flow field measurements, we identified two characteristic length scales, the ratio of flag area over its perimeter $L^*$ and the square root of area $\sqrt{HL}$ that scale the circulation of vortices shed per cycle. Values of the mean drag coefficient scatter widely, from \num{0} to \num{0.55}, when varying mass and aspect ratio. We can collapse the data when using a kinematics-based model with the mass ratio and the tip speed as inputs.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic shock waves: simultaneous accuracy of lower- and higher-order moments, with and without moment supervision
papers.abstract: We investigate physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for one-dimensional kinetic shock waves governed by the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) and Shakhov collision models, with and without moment supervision. The trace-free third-order and the fourth-order moments enter the fluxes of stress and heat flux through a shock; the aim, to our knowledge not previously examined for kinetic PINNs, is simultaneous accuracy of these and the lower-order moments of one predicted distribution. Data-assisted calculations, including anchor and closure studies, combine kinetic residuals with moment observations. For the BGK shock tube, a positive eight-moment representation whose spatial envelope follows the far-field decay of the initial condition gives heat-flux, stress and higher-moment discrepancies of $0.33\%$, $0.67\%$ and $1.8$--$2.0\%$ against the 6400-cell discrete-velocity method (DVM) reference supplying its observations; a five-field representation leaves the latter uncontrolled. Equation-trained characteristic-integral PINNs use analytic initial and incoming-boundary distributions and their own predicted moments. Their BGK and Shakhov shock-tube heat-flux and stress discrepancies are $0.41\%$ and $0.36\%$ against 3200-cell references; against the 6400-cell reference the BGK values are $0.21\%$ and $0.18\%$, and $0.4$--$0.9\%$ for the higher moments. Stationary neural continuation covers Shakhov Mach 2--5 and BGK Mach 6--7. Characteristic correction reduces the Mach-7 heat-flux and stress discrepancies from $3.37\%$ and $1.34\%$ to $0.42\%$ and $0.43\%$; at Mach~8 they are $0.62\%$ and $0.79\%$, and at Mach~12, across references, $0.40$--$1.03\%$ and $0.41$--$2.65\%$. Three independent Mach-2 initialisations assess repeatability. It is established that lower moments do not determine higher ones; the contribution is to quantify which moments each information regime recovers.

papers.title: Wave collapse proliferation as a mechanism for anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity
papers.abstract: Anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity are signatures of the roughness of the inviscid limit in fluid turbulence. Spontaneous stochasticity describes the selection of a probability distribution over possible solutions rather than a single deterministic trajectory. We investigate these phenomena in a nonlinear dispersive equation undergoing finite-time blowup, known as wave collapse. Collapse is arrested by two regularization mechanisms, one dissipative and one conservative. Heuristic arguments supported by numerical simulations show that an isolated collapse has a vanishing effect in the inviscid limit and cannot alone account for either phenomenon. However, simulations reveal that the number of collapse events diverges as the regularization vanishes. Their proliferation enables sustained dissipation in the dissipative case and prevents either regularization from selecting a single inviscid solution. We then introduce vanishingly small random perturbations and find numerical evidence for a well-defined statistical limit in which randomness persists. These results identify collapse proliferation as a mechanism connecting anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity in dispersive waves, allowing a formally deterministic equation to acquire a truly random limiting evolution.

papers.title: High-order immersed boundary method for subsonic aeroacoustics and compressible Navier-Stokes equations
papers.abstract: In computational fluid dynamics, the immersed boundary method is a classical technique to account for complex geometries when Cartesian grids are used, as is the case in finite difference methods. The present paper presents a new discrete ghost point method, which is one of the different immersed boundary methods available, for solving problems in acoustics and aeroacoustics with the linearized Euler equations or the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. This method is based on high-order schemes and a ghost point method. The flow field values at the ghost points are determined in two steps. A least-squares interpolation is first used to reconstruct the flow on a stencil of points located on the normal to the immersed boundary. Then, a 4th order Lagrangian extrapolation based on the normal stencil points adjacent to the boundary point is used to impose the boundary conditions at the immersed boundary by reconstructing the field values at the ghost points. This approach is verified and validated for the acoustical problem of a pressure pulse impinging on a cylinder. The approach is also validated for compressible flow past a circular cylinder at several Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Transition to turbulence in swirl created by a vertical magnetic field in liquid metal electrodes
papers.abstract: Flow transitions in electromagnetically-driven swirl in a cylindrical domain are investigated using three-dimensional simulations for a liquid metal battery electrode. The parameter space considered: applied current $I=11.11-100A$; Current density, $J_0 \approx 4,000-35,000 A/m^2$, domain radius, $R=3-9cm$, domain height, $H=3$ and $4.5cm$). The background magnetic field, $B_0$, strength is varied systematically from 0.1 to 20 G to characterize the route to chaos. Davidson et al. (2022) found the onset of chaos occurs around $1-1.5 G$ for aspect ratio $1/6$ and current of 100A, however, this is shifted to $16-17 G$ for a lower current of 16A and aspect ratio $1/2$. Across a range of geometrical configurations and forcing conditions, including variations in aspect ratio, current and current density, a consistent sequence of dynamical transitions is evident from phase portraits, FFT spectrum, 0-1 chaos test, autocorrelation function and correlation dimension. The flow evolution is by the Ruelle--Takens-Newhouse route to chaos, with the strange non-chaotic attractor (SNA) regime providing an intermediate state prior to the onset of chaos. In our results, it is observed that, for a fixed aspect ratio, the transition is governed by a dimensionless group, $Q_m$, representing the ratio of applied Lorentz force to viscous force. The critical value of $Q_m$ at the onset of oscillatory flow is found to be nearly invariant except when the domain height is varied. Moreover, our results follow the $Re \sim Q_m^{2/3}$ scaling law expected from torque balance moderately-forced electro-magnetically driven swirl flows.
